## Where and when did accidents happen?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
![](take-home-01/figures/locations.png){height=570 alt="Accident locations across the six Greater Bangkok provinces."}
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
The study covers 2022 and six provinces:

Bangkok, Nonthaburi, Pathum Thani, Nakhon Pathom, Samut Prakan and Samut Sakhon.

- Where do reports concentrate?
- How does that change during 2022?
- Does the pattern change when deaths are considered?
- Are nearby accidents also unusually close in time?

::: {.small-note}
Each record is an accident report, rather than a count of vehicles or casualties. Study period: 1 January to 31 December 2022.
:::
:::
:::

## Which records could I use?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.key-number}
3,599
:::

accident records with usable locations inside the study area.

Another 189 Bangkok reports have no coordinates. All came from the Expressway Authority, making up 43.1% of its Bangkok reports.
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
To prepare the records, I:

- kept 2022 records inside the six provinces;
- left reports without locations out of the maps;
- kept repeated locations and checked two possible duplicate pairs separately;
- used coordinates when province labels disagreed.

The three agencies report accidents on highways, rural roads and expressways. They do not cover every local street or every accident.
:::
:::

::: {.small-note}
Sources: [Ministry of Transport compilation via Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/thaweewatboy/thailand-road-accident-2019-2022) and [geoBoundaries country downloads](https://www.geoboundaries.org/countryDownloads.html) (Thailand, ADM1); downloaded 11 September 2026. Boundaries represent 2017.
:::

## Eastern Bangkok stands out

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="65%"}
![](take-home-01/figures/density.png){height=570 alt="Annual density map with the strongest smoothed peak in eastern Bangkok."}
:::
::: {.column width="35%"}
Eastern Bangkok has the highest density with all three bandwidths: 1, 2 and 4 km.

At 2 km, the peak is about 9.3 records per km² over the year.

More smoothing changes the outline and lowers the peak, but the same broad area stands out.

::: {.small-note}
The map uses Gaussian KDE, UTM 47N, 250 m cells and a boundary correction. To judge risk per journey, I would also need traffic volumes.
:::
:::
:::

## A closer look at Routes 7 and 9

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
![](take-home-01/figures/roads.png){height=550 alt="Accident density following Routes 7 and 9 in eastern Bangkok."}
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
In a 10 km by 10 km area around the eastern Bangkok peak, I could match 426 reports to roads.

Routes 7 and 9 account for about 86% of them.

Following the roads gives 240 pairs within 1 km and a week, compared with about 246 after shuffling the times (p = 0.676).

This local test gives no clear evidence of extra clustering in time.

::: {.small-note}
This is a closer look at one area. It uses main roads and connectors as mapped in January 2022, with distance measured in either direction.
:::
:::
:::

## Fatal reports tell a different story

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="65%"}
![](take-home-01/figures/severity-geography.png){height=420 alt="The smoothed peak shifts from eastern Bangkok for all reports to Pathum Thani for fatal reports."}

Motorcycles appear in 11.3% of reports but 50.3% of fatal reports.
:::
::: {.column width="35%"}
159 mapped reports involved at least one death, recording 177 deaths in total.

Pathum Thani and Samut Prakan together account for just over half of fatal reports.

Bangkok has half of all reports, but only 17.0% of fatal reports.

From midnight to 6 am, 8.5% of reports were fatal, compared with around 2 to 2.5% during daytime hours.
:::
:::

::: {.small-note}
Each map is scaled to its own group total, with the same 2 km smoothing and colour scale. These are patterns among reported accidents, not risk per journey. Two fatal reports without coordinates are excluded.
:::

## More reports towards the end of the year

![](take-home-01/figures/monthly.png){height=430 alt="Monthly reports per day, peaking in October with or without the reports lacking coordinates."}

October has the most mapped records: 394, or 12.7 per day. July has the most fatal reports (24).

::: {.small-note}
I divide monthly totals by the number of days. Adding the 189 reports without locations leaves the broad pattern unchanged. More years would be needed to check whether it repeats.
:::

## The increase was not the same everywhere

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
![](take-home-01/figures/quarters.png){height=575 alt="Quarterly density maps with one shared scale."}
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
Average reports per day:

| Province | Jan-Mar to Oct-Dec |
|---|---|
| Bangkok | 3.94 → 6.17 |
| Samut Sakhon | 0.39 → 1.67 |
| Pathum Thani | 1.27 → 1.41 |

Across all six provinces, reports involving injuries but no deaths rise from 2.99 to 4.63 per day.

::: {.small-note}
All maps use a 2 km bandwidth and the same colour scale, adjusted for quarter length. Changes in traffic or reporting could help explain the increase.
:::
:::
:::

## Do nearby accidents happen close together in time?

![](take-home-01/figures/pair-test.png){height=400 alt="Actual close-pair count compared with 999 shuffled patterns."}

There are 2,204 pairs within 1 km and 7 days. After shuffling the times, the average is 2,091. The actual count is 5.4% higher (p = 0.002).

::: {.small-note}
For this Knox-style test, I keep locations fixed and shuffle times within each agency and month 999 times, assuming those times can be swapped. Each pair counts once; an accident can belong to several pairs. The regional result cannot show that one accident causes another.
:::

## Does that result hold up?

| Check at 1 km / 7 days | Above the shuffled average | p-value |
|---|---:|---:|
| Main analysis | 5.4% | 0.002 |
| Remove two possible duplicates | 5.3% | 0.003 |
| Exclude identical-coordinate pairs | 4.9% | 0.003 |
| Shuffle within month only | 6.0% | 0.001 |

The duplicate and repeated-location checks give similar results.

Across nine combinations of distance and time, the actual counts are 2.7% to 17.1% above the shuffled averages. Allowing for all nine gives an overall p-value of 0.001.

::: {.small-note}
I checked 0.5, 1 and 2 km, each with 3, 7 and 14 days. After adjustment, eight comparisons have p-values below 0.05; 0.5 km / 7 days does not. Local traffic schedules or reporting changes could still affect the result.
:::

## Recommendations for road safety

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="53%"}
- Inspect Route 7 near Route 9 and the connecting ramps; repair any defects found.
- Include locations of fatal accidents in Pathum Thani, Samut Prakan and Nonthaburi when choosing sites to inspect.
- Review nighttime response coverage and motorcycle safety at these locations.
- Plan for the late-year rise in injury reports using recent accident and dispatch records.
- Review nearby accidents weekly and test any alert rule before adopting it.
- Require usable locations in reports and recover the missing expressway coordinates.
:::
::: {.column width="47%"}
The places with the most reports differ from those with the most fatal reports. Across the region, nearby accidents also happen within days of each other more often than the shuffled counts suggest.

It cannot tell us which areas account for this result, which roads are most dangerous, or what caused the pattern.

Check traffic volumes and conditions on site before changing patrol coverage or deciding on road improvements.
